opus-5.5.text:
I think there are really three layers to it.

The first is a strong base model with good multimodal perception. Operator works by looking at screenshots and deciding where to click and what to type, so the model has to understand a web page visually. It needs to read text in the image, locate buttons precisely, and ground language like "the search box in the top right" to actual pixel coordinates. That grounding ability is not trivial. A lot of earlier agents relied on parsing HTML or the accessibility tree. Going purely visual is more general, but it puts much more pressure on the vision side of the model.

The second, and I'd say the most important, is reinforcement learning. A pretrained model, even with supervised fine-tuning on human demonstrations, tends to be brittle in long-horizon tasks. Once it makes a small mistake, say it clicks the wrong thing and a pop-up appears, it's out of distribution and doesn't know how to recover. RL lets the model actually interact with environments, make mistakes, and learn from the outcome. That's how you get behaviors like noticing "this didn't work, let me go back and try another way." If you look at the progression from o1-style reasoning to Operator, the common thread is large-scale RL on top of a strong base model. Reasoning is RL in the space of thoughts. Agents are RL in the space of actions in a real environment.

The third is the infrastructure, which people often underestimate. To do RL for agents, you need a huge number of environments running in parallel: browsers, virtual machines, sandboxes. You need them to be reproducible, resettable, and safe. You also need reward signals. For web tasks that's hard, because "did you successfully book the right flight" isn't always easy to check automatically. So you need task design, verifiers, sometimes model-based judges. And the rollouts are long and slow, much slower than generating a math answer, so the training system has to handle asynchronous, long-trajectory rollouts efficiently. If your system waits for the slowest trajectory every step, your GPUs sit idle most of the time.

Beyond those three, there's a product-level ingredient: knowing when to hand control back to the human. For things like logging in, entering a payment, or confirming something irreversible, the agent should stop and ask. That's partly a safety design and partly a training target, because the model has to learn when it's uncertain or when an action is high-stakes.

So in short: a good multimodal base model, large-scale RL in real interactive environments, and a solid infrastructure for environments, rewards, and efficient training. I'd say the RL and infrastructure parts are where the real moat is right now. The base model capability is becoming more widely available, but making the agent actually robust over long tasks is mostly an RL and systems problem.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When people look at something like Operator, they tend to focus on the browser, the clicking, the visual interface. But I think the browser is actually the least important part. The hard part is underneath.

If I had to break it down, I'd say there are really four ingredients.

The first is the base model's ability to understand and act in a multimodal environment. An agent like this has to look at a screen, understand what's on it, and map that to an action. That sounds simple, but a screenshot of a webpage is a very noisy observation. There are ads, pop-ups, menus, elements that shift around. The model has to robustly ground language instructions to visual elements, and that grounding capability has to be trained in, not bolted on.

The second, and I think this is the core, is long-horizon decision making. Booking a flight or ordering groceries might take thirty or forty steps. At every step the model has to decide what to do next, and errors compound. If you have a ninety-five percent success rate per step, after thirty steps you're down to around twenty percent. So you need the model to be much more reliable per step than a chatbot needs to be, and you need it to recover from mistakes. That recovery ability, noticing you went down the wrong path and backtracking, is something that only really comes from reinforcement learning. You can't get it from imitation alone, because human demonstrations mostly show the successful path.

That brings me to the third ingredient, which is the environment and the data. To do RL you need environments where the agent can act, get feedback, and learn. For web agents this means you need sandboxed websites, or simulated versions of real sites, with well-defined reward signals. Did the task actually get completed? Building that infrastructure is enormous engineering work, and honestly I think it's where most of the real moat is. The algorithm matters, but the environment is what lets you scale.

And the fourth is safety and alignment in the agent setting. Once a model can actually take actions in the world, click buttons, spend money, send messages, the cost of a mistake goes up dramatically. So you need the model to know when to stop and ask the human. You need it to be robust to prompt injection, because a webpage could contain text trying to hijack the agent. These problems are different from chatbot alignment, and I think they're still fairly open.

So if someone asks me what the recipe is, I'd say: a strong multimodal base model, reinforcement learning for long-horizon tasks, a serious investment in environments and reward design, and a safety layer built specifically for agents that act. The browser interface is just the surface. Everything that matters is underneath.

astra-6.text:
I think there are three essential ingredients. The first is perception: the model needs to understand the interface—what’s on the screen, which elements are interactive, and what state the application is in. The second is action: it needs to translate that understanding into clicks, typing, and scrolling. The third is planning and feedback: it needs to keep track of the user’s goal, check whether an action worked, and recover when something goes wrong.

The real challenge is getting that whole loop to work reliably over many steps. A model can be very good at choosing a single action, but a task might require dozens of actions, and small errors accumulate. So you need training environments where the agent can interact, experience failures, and learn from the outcome, rather than only imitate successful demonstrations.

And then there’s knowing when to stop and ask the user. If an instruction is ambiguous or an action has significant consequences, recognizing that boundary is part of being a capable agent.

sol-6.1.text:
I would break it down into a few pieces. First, the model needs to understand what it sees on the screen and connect that to actions—where to click, what to type, and how to navigate. Second, it needs to reason over multiple steps. A user gives you a goal, but the interface doesn’t tell you the whole plan, so you have to act, observe the result, and adjust.

The third ingredient is training for that interaction loop. Learning from demonstrations is useful, but you also want the agent to learn from trying tasks and getting feedback on whether it actually succeeded. That requires environments where you can practice and evaluate reliably.

And then there’s reliability: recognizing mistakes, recovering from them, and knowing when to ask the user for clarification or confirmation. A convincing demo might follow one successful path. A useful agent has to handle all the unexpected things that happen along the way.
